newsitem.title: CHILE: German colony in Chile fears leader will kill himself.
newsitem.headline: German colony in Chile fears leader will kill himself.

text.p: The fugitive leader of a tight-knit German colony in southern Chile might commit suicide if police keep searching for him, his followers said, but police entered the community anyway on Thursday for the third day in a row.

Police in a convoy of seven vehicles drove past electrified barbed-wire gates into the colony in search of Paul Schaeffer, a former Nazi army officer, wanted on child abuse charges. They met no resistance.
Members of Schaeffer's Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) on Wednesday night issued a blistering letter accusing Chilean police of planning to kill him or drive him to suicide.

"There is nothing left but the murder announced by those officials (of the police) or a suicide," said the letter, distributed to reporters outside the colony, which is guarded by electrified fences and burly security agents.
The letter, handed to reporters by a Chilean member of the community on Wednesday night and read on state television on Thursday, was signed by "the elder women of Colonia Dignidad."
A leader of the community, Hartmutt Hopp, said the women were merely "expressing their fears" in the letter and that Schaeffer had not necessarily threatened to kill himself.
Nevertheless the letter gave the first public indication that Schaeffer, who founded the secretive colony around 1960, would sooner kill himself than allow police to arrest him.
Schaeffer issued a statement from hiding last week saying he feared for his life if he surrendered to police and alleging he could not get a fair trial in Chile.

The inspections, though with the acquiescence of settlers, were raising tensions inside the colony. A recording of church bells rang through the settlement each time the police entered and one distraught woman said the police moves felt like the Allied march on Germany at the end of the Second World War.

Residents say Schaeffer has not been seen for months in the colony, nestled among the Andean foothills about 200 miles (320 km) south of Santiago. Police were wasting their time looking for him there, they said.
"They can look all they want, he's not here," colony member Kurt Schnellenkamp told reporters in German-accented Spanish. "Give up? No, no. Why should he give up?"
Schaeffer, believed to be about 80, has an arrest-warrant against him since November on charges of child abuse, obstruction of justice and other charges.
The parents of at least five boys who attended a boarding school in the colony have filed charges of sexual abuse and illegal detention of the children against Schaeffer and other colony authorities.

With a modern hospital, traditional Bavarian homes, tidy farms and German-speaking settlers, the colony sprawls across scenic hills a few miles (kms) outside Parral, a town best-known as the birthplace of poet Pablo Neruda.

Residents are reported to number about 300. Apart from some Chilean workers, the residents speak little or no Spanish, rarely see visitors and lead isolated lives under the tight control of the colony's authorities, former residents say. They describe Schaeffer as a domineering man who allows no dissent in the community.

The colony was protected by the former military regime of Gen. Augusto Pinochet, and human rights groups have charged that the military used it as a secret detention and torture centre. In 1991 the Chilean government cancelled the colony's status as a charitable organisation.
